title: Nth Fibonacci Number
directAnswer: Iterate bottom-up keeping only the last two values for O(n) time and O(1) space. When n is huge, use fast doubling (or matrix exponentiation) to compute F(n) in O(log n) via the identities F(2k) = F(k)·(2F(k+1) − F(k)) and F(2k+1) = F(k)² + F(k+1)².

remember.pattern: Bottom-up two-variable iteration; fast doubling for O(log n)
remember.formula:
# O(n) iterative
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
    a, b = b, a + b
return a

# O(log n) fast doubling identities
F(2k)   = F(k) * (2*F(k+1) - F(k))
F(2k+1) = F(k)^2 + F(k+1)^2
rules: Never write naive recursion `fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` — it's O(φⁿ) and recomputes the same values exponentially. Memoize or iterate.
Pin down the indexing convention: this page uses F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1. Off-by-one here flips every answer.
Fibonacci overflows fast — F(93) exceeds a signed 64-bit `long`. Use BigInteger (Java) for large n; Python ints are unbounded.
The iterative version needs only **two** rolling variables, not a full DP array — O(1) space.
Fast doubling beats matrix exponentiation in constant factors (no 2×2 multiplies) while sharing the same O(log n) bound.
whenToUse: Compute a single F(n) — iterative O(n) is the clean default
n is astronomically large and you need O(log n) → fast doubling / matrix power
Teaching the memoization-vs-tabulation progression in DP
Any linear recurrence where you only need the last few terms (roll the window)
antiSignals: You need *all* F(0..n) → keep the array; don't recompute each
n is tiny and fixed → a lookup table is simplest
You need F(n) mod m for huge n → fast doubling under the modulus (Pisano period optional)
remember.takeaway: Fibonacci is the canonical 'naive recursion is exponential, but it collapses to O(n) with two variables and O(log n) with doubling' story. Showing that full ladder — and naming the overflow boundary — is what an interviewer is grading.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize naive recursion is exponential, reach for the O(1)-space iterative form, and — for the medium bar — know that an O(log n) method exists and why.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Submitting exponential recursion, getting the F(0)/F(1) base case off by one, or overflowing a long around F(93) without noticing.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Walk the full ladder: exponential recursion → memoized O(n) → iterative O(n) O(1) space → fast doubling O(log n). State the overflow point and offer BigInteger.

problemStatement:
Return the `n`-th Fibonacci number, where `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1`, and `F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2)` for `n ≥ 2`.

Discuss how your approach scales as `n` grows and what happens to the return type.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 92 if the answer must fit in a signed 64-bit integer
0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ or beyond with BigInteger / arbitrary precision
understanding: Each term is the sum of the two before it. You only ever need the previous two values to produce the next, so the whole sequence can be walked with constant memory — and a doubling identity skips most of the work entirely.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What indexing — does F(0) = 0 or F(1) = 1 start the sequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll use F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1. The convention matters because an off-by-one shifts every value; I'd confirm yours.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If n stays under ~92, a long holds F(n). Beyond that I switch to BigInteger, or use fast doubling if n is huge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want F(n) exactly, or modulo something?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If it's F(n) mod m for enormous n, I'd run fast doubling under the modulus rather than computing the full number.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a single value needed, or the whole prefix?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If you need every F(0..n) I'd keep the array; for a single value the two-variable roll is enough.

examples.explanation: F(93) exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE (~9.2 × 10¹⁸), so a long-based answer overflows — BigInteger required.

approaches.name: Iterative Bottom-Up, Two Variables (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean default — mention naive recursion is exponential, then jump straight to this O(1)-space loop.
hints: Naive recursion recomputes fib(n-2) over and over. What's the minimum history you actually need to produce the next term?
Just the previous two values. Carry a = F(i-1), b = F(i), and roll them forward n times.
Start a, b = 0, 1 and repeat a, b = b, a + b. After n rolls, a holds F(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: One loop of n iterations, each doing a constant-time addition and reassignment. Only two scalars are stored, so space is O(1) — no DP array needed.
approaches.explanation:
Build the sequence from the bottom, carrying only the two most recent values. Seed `a = F(0) = 0` and `b = F(1) = 1`, then repeat `(a, b) = (b, a + b)` exactly `n` times; `a` then holds `F(n)`.

**Why naive recursion is a trap.** Writing `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` looks like the definition, but it rebuilds the same subtrees over and over — `fib(n-2)` is computed twice, `fib(n-3)` three times, and so on. The call count grows like `φⁿ` (golden-ratio base), so `fib(50)` already takes seconds. Mention it only to dismiss it.

**Why two variables suffice.** The recurrence reaches back exactly two terms. Once you've produced `F(i)`, you never need anything older than `F(i-1)` again. So a full `dp[]` array is wasted memory — two rolling scalars capture all the state, dropping space from O(n) to O(1). This 'roll the window' move generalizes to any fixed-depth linear recurrence.

**Why the loop runs n times and a is the answer.** Start `(a, b)` as `(F(0), F(1))`. Each roll advances the window by one index: after one roll `a = F(1)`, after two `a = F(2)`, …, after `n` rolls `a = F(n)`. Returning `a` (not `b`) is the off-by-one most people get wrong — trace the first couple of iterations to be sure.

**Why overflow still bites.** Fibonacci grows exponentially (~`φⁿ`), so it blows past a 64-bit `long` at `F(93)`. The loop is correct, but the *type* must widen to `BigInteger` for large `n`. In Python this is automatic; in Java, say it out loud.
approaches.insight: You only need the last two terms, so the natural-looking DP array collapses to two variables and O(1) space. That window-rolling instinct — keep only what the recurrence references — is the reusable idea, not Fibonacci itself.

dryRun.intro: Seed (a, b) = (0, 1) and roll a, b = b, a + b six times; a ends as F(6).

This sum overflows a 64-bit long once n exceeds 92 — switch to BigInteger.
Return a, NOT b — the classic off-by-one is returning b (which is F(n+1)).

After n rolls a is F(n).

approaches.name: Fast Doubling (Optimal, O(log n))
approaches.whenToMention: When n is astronomically large or the interviewer pushes past O(n). Cite the doubling identities.
hints: The iterative method does n additions. Could you jump from F(k) straight to F(2k), halving the index each step like fast exponentiation?
Yes — there are identities expressing F(2k) and F(2k+1) purely in terms of F(k) and F(k+1).
Recurse on n >> 1 (n / 2), get (F(k), F(k+1)), then combine: F(2k) = F(k)·(2F(k+1) − F(k)), F(2k+1) = F(k)² + F(k+1)². Pick the right pair based on the low bit of n.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each recursive call halves n (processes one bit), so there are O(log n) calls; each does a constant number of multiplications. With fixed-width ints those multiplies are O(1), giving O(log n); with BigInteger the multiplies grow, but the call count is still log n.
approaches.explanation:
Compute `F(n)` by halving the index instead of decrementing it — the same trick that turns exponentiation into O(log n). Each level computes `(F(k), F(k+1))` from `(F(k/2), F(k/2 + 1))` using two closed-form identities.

**The identities and why they work.** From the matrix form of Fibonacci you can derive:

- `F(2k) = F(k) · (2·F(k+1) − F(k))`
- `F(2k+1) = F(k)² + F(k+1)²`

Given the pair at index `k`, these produce the pair at index `2k` in a constant number of multiplications. Because doubling the index each step covers `n` in `log₂ n` doublings, the whole computation is logarithmic.

**Why we track a *pair*, not a single value.** Both identities need `F(k)` *and* `F(k+1)` to step to the next level. So the recursion returns the tuple `(F(k), F(k+1))`; at each return we compute the doubled pair and then, if the current bit of `n` is `1`, shift by one more (the `(F(2k+1), F(2k) + F(2k+1))` adjustment) to land on the correct index. Read `n` bit by bit from the most significant end.

**Why it beats matrix exponentiation in practice.** Matrix exponentiation raises `[[1,1],[1,0]]` to the `n`-th power, also O(log n), but each step does eight scalar multiplies for the 2×2 product. Fast doubling does just a few multiplies per level for the *same* asymptotic bound, so it wins on constant factors and is less error-prone to code. Mention both; prefer doubling.

**Why O(log n) is a refinement, not free.** For large `n` the numbers themselves are huge (BigInteger), so each multiply isn't truly O(1). The honest claim is O(log n) *arithmetic operations*; the bit-complexity is higher. Still vastly better than O(n) additions on giant numbers.
approaches.insight: Fibonacci satisfies a doubling recurrence, so the same divide-the-exponent strategy behind fast power applies to the index. Recognizing that a linear recurrence has a logarithmic shortcut — via matrix power or these identities — is the medium-level signal.

double index 1→2 then shift on set bit → (F(3), F(4)) = (2, 3)

java.explanation: Recurse on n/2 — each level halves the index, giving O(log n) depth.
F(2k) = F(k)·(2F(k+1) − F(k)); shiftLeft(1) is the ×2.
Odd index: shift the pair up by one position.

python.explanation: Get (F(k/2), F(k/2 + 1)) from the halved index.
When the bit is set, advance one index further.

edgeCases.behavior: Base case returns the pair (0, 1); fib returns 0.
Recurses to n=0, doubles+shifts to (1, 1); returns 1.
Exceeds a long; BigInteger returns the exact 12200160415121876738.

pitfalls: Mixing up which identity is F(2k) vs F(2k+1).
Forgetting the odd-bit shift, landing one index off.
Claiming flat O(log n) for big n — the BigInteger multiplies themselves grow.

commonMistakes: Using exponential naive recursion instead of iterating or memoizing.
Returning F(n+1) instead of F(n) (off-by-one in the base/return).
Overflowing a long at F(93) without switching to BigInteger.
Building a full DP array when two rolling variables suffice.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Exponential naive recursion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) recomputes overlapping subproblems, giving O(φⁿ) calls. Memoize or iterate.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one on the return value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After n rolls of (a, b) = (b, a+b), a holds F(n) and b holds F(n+1). Returning b shifts every answer up by one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Silent long overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: F(93) exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE, so the addition wraps to a wrong value. Use BigInteger when n can exceed 92.

followupVariations.title: Climbing Stairs
followupVariations.hint: The number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps is exactly F(n+1) — same recurrence.

followupVariations.title: Fibonacci modulo m (Pisano period)
followupVariations.hint: F(n) mod m is periodic; combine fast doubling under the modulus with the Pisano period for enormous n.

followupVariations.title: Tribonacci / k-bonacci
followupVariations.hint: Roll a window of the last k values; matrix exponentiation generalizes the O(log n) idea.

patternNote: Linear recurrence solved bottom-up (window rolling for O(1) space) and via index-halving identities for O(log n). The transferable instincts: collapse a DP array to the few terms the recurrence references, and recognize that linear recurrences have logarithmic shortcuts through matrix power or doubling.
